content: Caspofungin is a medication used to treat various fungal infections, including candidemia and other Candida-related infections such as intra-abdominal abscesses, peritonitis, and pleural space infections. It is also indicated for esophageal candidiasis, invasive aspergillosis in patients who are intolerant or unresponsive to other therapies, and for empirical treatment of presumed fungal infections in febrile, neutropenic patients. For candidemia and other Candida infections, the treatment begins with a loading dose of 70 mg administered intravenously over one hour on the first day, followed by a maintenance dose of 50 mg IV daily, also infused over one hour. Antifungal therapy should continue for at least 14 days after the last positive culture. In patients with persistent neutropenia, a longer course of therapy may be required until neutropenia resolves. For esophageal candidiasis, the recommended dose is 50 mg IV daily, infused over one hour, for 7 to 14 days after symptom resolution. A loading dose is not necessary for this indication. In patients with HIV, suppressive oral therapy may be considered to prevent relapse of oropharyngeal candidiasis. For invasive aspergillosis in patients refractory to or intolerant of other therapies (e.g., amphotericin B, itraconazole), the initial dose is 70 mg IV on the first day, followed by 50 mg IV daily. The duration of treatment depends on the severity of the underlying disease, recovery from immunosuppression, and clinical response. In febrile, neutropenic patients with presumed fungal infections, the initial dose is 70 mg IV on the first day, followed by 50 mg IV daily. If the response is inadequate but the drug is well-tolerated, the dose may be increased to 70 mg IV daily. Empirical therapy should continue until neutropenia resolves. If a fungal infection is confirmed, treatment should last for a minimum of 14 days and continue for at least 7 days after both neutropenia and clinical symptoms have resolved. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends echinocandins, such as caspofungin, as initial therapy for Candida auris infections. Pediatric dosing is based on body surface area, with limited data suggesting an off-label dose of 25 mg/m² IV daily for infants under 3 months of age, although safety and efficacy in this population are not well established. Caspofungin interacts with several drugs, including cyclosporine, rifampin, and certain statins, among others. These interactions may increase or decrease caspofungin levels or enhance the risk of adverse effects such as myopathy or nephrotoxicity. Close monitoring or dose adjustments may be necessary when co-administered with these agents. Adverse effects of caspofungin include infusion-related reactions (e.g., rash, facial swelling, pruritus, or bronchospasm), fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, headache, and injection site reactions. Serious reactions, such as anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, hepatic dysfunction, and renal impairment, have been reported. Patients should be monitored for signs of hypersensitivity or worsening liver function during therapy. Caspofungin is administered intravenously, typically once daily over one hour. It should not be used with dextrose diluents or administered as a bolus. Proper preparation and storage of the medication are essential, and it should be used within specified timeframes after reconstitution. During pregnancy, caspofungin should only be used if clearly needed, as there is insufficient data to determine its safety. It is unknown whether the drug passes into human breast milk, so the benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against potential risks to the infant. Patients should complete the full prescribed course of therapy, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Regular monitoring of liver and kidney function, as well as potassium levels, is recommended during treatment.
